description.summary: Memgraph is a Cypher-compatible property-graph database with native node and edge vector indexes, text search, streaming ingestion, graph algorithms, and GraphRAG tooling; its USearch-backed HNSW-style vector subsystem uses READ_UNCOMMITTED isolation and must be evaluated separately from ordinary graph transaction guarantees.
description.description: Memgraph is a real-time property-graph database that exposes Cypher-compatible querying, multiple storage modes, streaming ingestion, full-text search, MAGE graph algorithms, replication, and deployment across local, self-hosted, Kubernetes, Enterprise, and cloud environments. Its native vector-search feature supports vector indexes on nodes and edges. Index definitions specify dimension, capacity, similarity metric, scalar representation, and label or edge-type scope, while vector_search procedures return approximate nearest neighbors for explicit composition with Cypher traversals, graph properties, text-search results, and algorithms. Memgraph documents a single-store vector design backed by USearch: the vector index owns the vector payload and the property store retains a reference rather than duplicating the same embedding. This architecture makes connected vector retrieval practical, but it also creates important operational boundaries. The query planner does not currently select vector indexes automatically, vector-index isolation is READ_UNCOMMITTED, and graph, text, vector, and algorithm scores require explicit application-level fusion or ranking. The main database can provide stronger transaction and durability behavior according to storage mode, WAL, snapshots, replication, and edition, yet those guarantees must not be projected automatically onto the vector subsystem. Memgraph is therefore most compelling when graph structure, streaming updates, connected context, or graph algorithms materially improve retrieval quality or explainability; a dedicated vector service may be simpler when graph relationships add no decision value.

indexingConsiderations: Version the embedding model, vector dimension, metric, scalar kind, index capacity, label or edge-type scope, Memgraph version, edition, and storage mode as one ingestion contract.
Create separate node and edge vector indexes only where each search surface has an explicit retrieval use case and evaluation set.
Treat index labels, edge types, and wildcard scope as index-design choices rather than assuming arbitrary query-time metadata prefiltering.
Size graph data, vector indexes, text indexes, transaction working sets, MAGE algorithms, WAL, snapshots, and replicas together because they compete for memory, CPU, disk, and recovery time.
Keep authoritative source text and a reproducible embedding pipeline so indexes can be rebuilt after model, dimension, scalar, capacity, or schema changes.
retrievalConsiderations: Invoke vector_search procedures explicitly because the query planner does not currently choose vector indexes automatically.
Evaluate node-vector, edge-vector, text-only, graph-only, vector-plus-traversal, text-plus-graph, and algorithm-augmented retrieval on the same relevance set.
Calibrate vector similarity, text relevance, traversal heuristics, and graph-algorithm scores explicitly instead of treating them as directly comparable.
Measure whether label or edge-type index scope and subsequent Cypher filtering reduce candidate completeness or return fewer than the requested top-k.
Test vector-index visibility, retries, and repair procedures independently because vector indexes use READ_UNCOMMITTED isolation.
Tune top-k, graph expansion depth, path constraints, text candidate windows, algorithm concurrency, and stream-update rate against relevance, latency, and memory budgets.

limitations: Vector indexes use READ_UNCOMMITTED isolation, so their visibility and consistency boundaries are weaker than ordinary graph transaction guarantees.
The query planner does not currently utilize vector indexes automatically; applications must call the vector_search procedures explicitly.
Vector search is approximate and depends on embedding geometry, dimension, metric, scalar representation, index capacity, memory pressure, and workload concurrency.
Index label or edge-type scope and post-search Cypher composition are not equivalent to arbitrary in-index query-time metadata prefiltering.
Graph, vector, text, and algorithm scores are not automatically normalized or fused into a universal hybrid ranking.
On-disk transactional graph storage does not imply disk-backed vector indexing; vector memory must be sized separately.
Native sharding is not represented as supported by this record; horizontal scale relies primarily on deployment topology, replication, and workload partitioning.
High availability, advanced security, multi-tenancy, support, and managed operations vary by Community, Enterprise, and cloud offering.
Official Memgraph documentation does not replace independent recall, latency, durability, cost, or recovery benchmarking.
usageGuidance: Use Memgraph when RAG or agent retrieval benefits materially from semantic similarity combined with explicit relationships, paths, streaming updates, graph algorithms, or connected memory.
Use native node and edge vector indexes when keeping embeddings close to the graph reduces integration complexity and enables direct Cypher expansion from retrieved candidates.
Prefer a dedicated vector or search service when graph relationships, graph algorithms, and connected explanations do not improve retrieval quality enough to justify graph operational complexity.
Prefer an RDF or SPARQL-oriented graph system when RDF semantics, standards-based ontology reasoning, or SPARQL compatibility are mandatory.
Record Memgraph version, edition, deployment, storage mode, vector-index definition, embedding model, query procedures, text-search configuration, and MAGE algorithms in every evaluation.
